problem: The pointer direction is stated backwards. The bullet says each copy of the right keeps a pointer back to the file's entry, and that to revoke the system follows the pointers and deletes every copy. Pointers from copy to object lead the wrong way: following them from a copy cannot find the other copies. This contradicts worked example 1 step 2, where the bob entry itself carries four pointers to the copies, and contradicts the standard description of the scheme.
fix: Each object keeps a list of back-pointers, one pointer to every copy of a right held on it. To revoke, the system follows the pointers stored with the object and deletes each copy they name. The cost is one step per copy, and one missed pointer leaves a live right.

where: Worked example 1, step 1 and step 5, and Quiz Q4 part (a)
problem: The example counts access-list revocation as a complete 1 step even though the stem says bob's read right has already been copied into P1, P4, P9 and P12. Deleting the bob entry stops future checks only. The four processes already hold the right (for example open file descriptors) and keep reading the payroll file. A student reads '1 step' as 'the four copies die', which is exactly the confusion the chapter warns about elsewhere. The same flaw is in Q4, where 6 processes are said to hold the right and the answer is still 1 step.
fix: Say that the access list is cheap only because the check is redone at every access: deleting the bob entry is 1 step and blocks all later opens and re-checks, but rights already handed out (open handles, passed descriptors) stay live and must be closed or invalidated separately. In the counts, state the 1 step as '1 step, and it covers only future accesses; the four live copies are not reached'. Fix Q4 part (a) the same way: 1 step for the entry, plus the copies still alive unless the system re-checks each access.
